✻ Worked for 42s · done 9:36 PM

❯ Write a single 300-word paragraph about the history of git worktrees. Plain prose, no lists, no headings, no tools.

⏺ Git worktrees arrived in Git 2.5, released in July 2015, after Nathaniel Wilson's work on a git worktree command that let a single
  repository hold several working directories at once. Before that, developers who needed two branches checked out at the same time had to
  clone the repository again or juggle stashes and branch switches, which was slow for large projects and error-prone when a half-finished
  change got in the way of an urgent fix. The new command kept one shared object database and one set of references while giving each
  linked worktree its own index and HEAD, so a clone was no longer needed just to look at another branch. The first versions were fairly
  minimal: git worktree add created a new directory tied to a branch, and git worktree list showed what existed. Over the following
  releases the command gained more safeguards and conveniences. Git began refusing to check out the same branch in two worktrees unless
  forced, which prevented silent conflicts over a shared ref. Later versions added git worktree remove, git worktree prune for cleaning up
  entries whose directories had been deleted by hand, and git worktree lock for keeping a worktree on removable storage from being pruned.
  Support for per-worktree configuration arrived with extensions.worktreeConfig, which let settings differ between checkouts while still
  sharing the repository's common configuration. Tooling built on top of worktrees followed, including editor integrations and continuous
  integration scripts that spin up disposable checkouts for each job. Today the feature is a standard part of many workflows, especially
  for reviewing pull requests, running long builds in parallel with ongoing edits, and working on several releases at once without
  repeatedly rebuilding the same project from scratch.
